newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Embittered Bhutto moves out of official mansion.
newsitem.headline: Embittered Bhutto moves out of official mansion.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, surrounded by chanting supporters, moved out of her official residence into a private home on Tuesday, a week after being sacked on disputed charges of corruption.

"I think this whole thing stinks," an embittered Bhutto told an impromptu news conference at the home of Senator Gulzar Ahmed, where she will temporarily stay with her three children after vacating the prime minister's mansion.
Her husband, Asif Ali Zardari, who was investment minister in the ousted government, has been held without charge under a maintenance of public order law since Bhutto's dismissal.

About 200 activists from her Pakistan People's Party mobbed the black BMW sedan carrying Bhutto after it passed through the iron gates outside the prime minister's residence on its way to Ahmed's house in the capital Islamabad.

A crowd quickly surrounded the car, forcing it to stop. "Go, Leghari, go!" the activists shouted, denouncing President Farooq Leghari, who dissolved the National Assembly and dismissed Bhutto's three-year-old government last week.
"Benazir step forward, we are with you!" the party workers chanted before the car sped off to Ahmed's house, a short distance away, where dozens of supporters forced their way in.
Bhutto, holding her three-year-old daughter Asifa on her lap, told reporters her lawyers expected to file a petition on Wednesday morning asking the Supreme Court to reinstate her.
"I look forward to early relief by the Supreme Court. I repudiate the charges the president has made," she said.
Bhutto lashed Leghari, demanding that he step down as president. "I do not expect fair elections from Leghari," she said, referring to parliamentary polls set for February 3.

She said he had made "foul accusations" in his dismissal order which cited corruption and misrule and which said Bhutto had insinuated that the presidency conspired to murder her brother Murtaza, who was gunned down on September 20.

"This convinces me that directly or indirectly, there is a nexus between my brother's death and the president," she said. She asked why the president had "sacked" British detectives whom she had brought in to investigate the case.
"I say, Leghari, if your hands are clean, why have you sacked the British detectives?" she said.
"He struck in the middle of the night," she said, referring to Leghari's midnight order dismissing her. "Only thieves strike in the night."
Bhutto said her dismissal and forced move were traumatic for her staff and children.
"But since this is the third time around with me, and because I had been hearing so many reports...I was actually mentally geared up to the whole thing," she said.

She was ousted in 1990 on similar charges. Her father, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, was Pakistan's first popularly elected prime minister, ruling from 1971 to 1977 when he was toppled by army chief General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq.
Zulfikar was hanged in April 1979 on a disputed conviction for conspiring to commit a political murder.
"I suppose that life has made me a bit tough," Benazir said.
"I haven't had an easy life, and for the last 20 years that I have been in politics, life has been very difficult. I've had my share of triumphs and I've had my share of tragedies."
